items.title: Global Biodiversity Framework at risk of becoming an empty promise
items.desc: The landmark Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed upon in 2022, was a major step forward in tackling global biodiversity loss. But without consistent, scientifically robust measures of progress, its ambitions risk going unrealized, a global collaboration of scientists has argued.

items.title: Physicists send an unblockable message using gravity
items.desc: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

items.title: Damaged rocks may help explain why small earthquakes outnumber large ones
items.desc: University of Michigan researchers have developed a better way to understand why earthquakes occur and what size they might be. Currently, models that predict earthquakes only account for slipping that occurs along a main fault, activity that usually generates large earthquakes. Instead, the U-M researchers have built a model that considers not only the main fault action but also the activity of rocks that lie adjacent to the fault and become damaged during earthquake events.

items.title: Water purification method turns old batteries into magnetic pollutant traps
items.desc: How can harmful substances be removed from water? When it comes to dyes that cannot simply be filtered out, this is usually very laborious: You need substances to which the dyes attach, and then the water often has to be painstakingly centrifuged.

items.title: How cells use alternative genetic instructions to produce 'shadowing proteins'
items.desc: The human genome contains tens of thousands of genes that provide instructions for making the proteins responsible for carrying out essential functions throughout the body. But those instructions may be more versatile than scientists once understood.

items.title: Strange radio signals from space could come from a dead star
items.desc: The night sky is as good a place as any for a mystery. Back in 2002, astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves coming from near the center of our galaxy, spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. The signals were detected again in 2003 and 2004, but then disappeared. Despite years of searching, there was no sign of their return.

items.title: Researchers review isotope methods for tracing and quantifying gaseous nitrogen production in soils
items.desc: Researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology (IAE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reviewed stable nitrogen isotope techniques for tracing the sources and quantifying the production of gaseous nitrogen in soils. The review examines four approaches for distinguishing microbial pathways that produce nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO) and dinitrogen (N₂).

items.title: Stem cell–derived nanoparticles modulate immune cells and help delay type 1 diabetes in mice
items.desc: In people with type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly identifies insulin-producing cells in the pancreas as foreign and attacks them, leaving the body unable to properly regulate blood sugar. While insulin therapy helps manage the disease, it does not stop the underlying immune attack.

items.title: Bolivia's Madidi National Park shelters 99 bat species, including 7 new to the country
items.desc: A new study has confirmed 100 bat taxa in Madidi National Park, in northwestern Bolivia, including 99 recognized species and one that may be new to science. The park is home to 68% of the bat species known from Bolivia.

items.title: Making diversity count: New paper highlights overlooked scientists in the chemical sciences curriculum
items.desc: A new paper by James Wilton-Ely, Ravi Singh and collaborators explores how curriculum diversification can help address the underrepresentation of minority-background scientists in chemical sciences education.

items.title: Record ocean warming hundreds of meters below B.C. coast linked to El Niño
items.desc: Scientists are observing record ocean temperatures off the British Columbia coast, with temperatures spiking as much as 2.5 degrees Celsius above the long-term averages recorded at Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) seafloor observatory sites—indicating the arrival of El Niño impacts on Canada's Pacific coastline.

items.title: Bee-lieve it or not, bumblebees have a sweet spot for salt
items.desc: Minerals are vital for bumblebee health, but too much can be harmful. For this new study, which is published in Royal Society Open Science, researchers tested how buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) responded to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium and sodium in artificial nectar.

items.title: Writing changes language less than we think
items.desc: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history. It transformed how we share knowledge, communicate and pass information from one generation to the next. But has it also changed the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages?

items.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
items.desc: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.

items.title: From 'paper parks' to real protection: Guide offers steps to support marine protected areas
items.desc: As the world works toward protecting 30% of the planet's land and sea by 2030, the study highlights why the success of marine protected areas (MPAs) depends not just on how much ocean is designated for protection, but on how these areas are planned, governed, monitored and enforced.

items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.desc: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
items.desc: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

items.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
items.desc: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.desc: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.desc: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.desc: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.

items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
items.desc: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
items.desc: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.desc: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

items.title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
items.desc: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.desc: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

items.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
items.desc: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.desc: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

items.title: Demography is the Achilles’ Heel of Dictatorships
items.desc: Governments that manipulate population figures often end up deceiving themselves as much as the public. When autocratic leaders mistake inflated numbers for real national strength, they make costly strategic mistakes and fail to address their countries’ demographic decline until it is too late.

items.title: The Silver Lining of a Data-Center Slowdown
items.desc: With leading AI labs under intense competitive pressure to keep advancing the frontier of the technology's capabilities, resistance to the build-out of computing resources is not such a bad thing. The more time we can buy, the greater our chances of maximizing the potential benefits and mitigating the risks.

items.title: What Nvidia’s Crisis Reveals About the Chip War
items.desc: Export restrictions, like those depriving China of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, may buy time by curtailing a competitor's access to frontier capabilities made elsewhere. But in any technological conflict, policymakers must remember that slowing a rival is not the same as strengthening oneself.

items.title: When Export Restraints Are the Lesser Evil
items.desc: Governments face pressure to protect domestic industries while preserving access to cheaper foreign goods. The recent EU-China car-export deal offers an uneasy compromise that protects European automakers while keeping Chinese cars available to consumers, making it preferable to prohibitive tariffs.

items.title: The Trade Losses That Nobody Counts
items.desc: While much of the United Kingdom’s post-Brexit debate has focused on the monetary value of lost trade with the European Union, the composition of UK-EU trade flows warrants closer attention. A sharp decline in the variety of products shipped to Europe suggests that the economic costs have been greater than many realize.

items.title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
items.desc: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

items.title: What Should the Nvidia Board Do?
items.desc: The proper role of any corporate board is to strike a careful balance between stakeholders. In Nvidia's case, the board will have to consider not just the current trading price, but also how its decisions will affect the landscape in which it operates, its employees, and its license to trade.

items.title: The Roots of Macron’s Failure
items.desc: Although French President Emmanuel Macron has certainly made mistakes, his troubled presidency is symptomatic of a deeper problem. In the end, he failed to build something truly enduring because he was seduced by the same monarchical impulse that is a recurring feature of French political culture.

items.title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
items.desc: In principle, the planned summit of the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else.

items.title: The Perverse Effects of the AI Investment Boom
items.desc: As big tech companies increasingly turn to debt markets to finance massive investments in AI data centers, they are competing for the same pools of capital as many governments. With interest rates already high and public demands for spending on the rise, the timing could hardly be worse for vulnerable economies.

items.title: Oceania’s Three Goals for COP31
items.desc: To make COP31 the “Blue COP,” delegates must recommit to keeping the 1.5° Celsius warming goal alive, reform the climate-finance system, and address our dependence on the fossil fuels driving the ocean's warming and acidification. Pacific countries have long championed these causes, but now the rest of the world must join them.

items.title: America After the Midterms
items.desc: The Democrats came out on top in the midterms by staying on message and focusing on affordability. But from voters’ perspective, there is an enormous difference between repudiating the administration and embracing the alternative.

items.title: Can Brexit Be Reversed?
items.desc: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Brexit a mistake, and opinion polls show that his proposal to "go all the way" and rejoin the European Union has majority support. But Brexit was won by a movement, and only a movement can reverse it.

items.title: Portfolio Regime Change?
items.desc: Rather than assuming that traditional asset-allocation guidelines apply to current conditions, investors should position themselves for more volatility and uncertainty. The AI revolution and various structural forces mean that there is no going back to the familiar old diversification formula.

items.title: The Global Economy After the Iran War Ends
items.desc: Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.
